title: Result and Either patterns for typed errors
hook: Exceptions hide failure paths in the type signature. A Result type makes success and failure explicit in the return type — callers must handle both. This is how you model expected failures without stack walks on hot paths.

blocks.text: A **Result** (sometimes called **Either** in functional libraries) is a **discriminated union** that represents either success or failure without throwing. The canonical TypeScript shape is `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }`. The **ok** field is the discriminant — TypeScript narrows `value` or `error` after you check `ok`. Unlike exceptions, failures appear in the function signature: `parseRow(line: string): Result<CsvRow, ParseError>`. Callers cannot ignore the error branch without a compile-time smell (unchecked result).

entries.plainDefinition: A union type encoding success (value) or failure (error) as data instead of control flow via throw.
entries.example: type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

entries.plainDefinition: Functional name for left-or-right outcomes. Left is often failure, right is success — convention varies by library.
entries.example: Either<ParseError, CsvRow> — error on left, value on right.

entries.plainDefinition: A union with a shared literal field (ok, kind, type) so switch and if narrow correctly.
Chaining Result-returning steps so an early failure skips later work — like a train switching tracks.

blocks.text: Parsing a million-row CSV where 2% of rows are malformed is not exceptional — it is expected. Throwing and catching per bad row allocates and walks the stack. Returning `Result<CsvRow, string>` keeps control flow flat and lets you count failures in metrics. At API boundaries (HTTP handlers, CLI tools, library public surfaces), Result documents what can go wrong without reading the implementation. C# teams often use TryParse or a small Result struct for the same reason — TypeScript gets it from unions with zero runtime overhead when inlined.

blocks.title: When Result beats throw
blocks.body: Validation, not-found, parse errors, and business-rule rejections are expected outcomes. Reserve throw for programmer bugs, unrecoverable I/O, and invariant violations you cannot represent as data.

items.title: Return Result from the boundary function
items.body: parseRow returns ok: false with a typed error instead of throw on bad input.

items.title: Chain with map / flatMap
items.body: Each step returns Result; early failure short-circuits the chain.

items.title: Convert to throw at the outer edge if needed
items.body: HTTP layer may throw 400 after Result says validation failed — one conversion point.

blocks.title: Result everywhere including BCL-style I/O
blocks.body: Wrapping every fs.readFile and fetch in Result adds noise. Wrap at your domain boundary; let low-level APIs throw and catch once at the edge.

blocks.title: Ignoring the error branch
blocks.body: const v = result.value without checking ok compiles poorly and fails at runtime. Use if (!result.ok) return or exhaustive switch.

blocks.text: Result<T, E> is erased at runtime — enforcement is compile-time only, unlike Rust's Result. Choose E as a small union of codes (not-a-number | out-of-range) or a discriminated error type for exhaustiveness. For async, return Promise<Result<T, E>> or use async functions that return Result directly. At boundaries, convert Result to HTTP status once: validation err → 400, not-found → 404. Do not pull a 200 KB functional library for a twenty-line union — interviewers prefer a minimal ok/err. Measure: exception rate vs Result failure rate in import jobs; Result should dominate on expected paths.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming Result replaces all exceptions with no tradeoffs. Using Result but never checking ok. Importing heavy Either libraries for a simple union. Not knowing TypeScript erases Result at runtime.

interviewTakeaways: Result is a discriminated union — ok: true carries value, ok: false carries typed error.
Use Result for expected failures (validation, parse, not-found); throw for exceptional paths.
Chain with map/flatMap; convert to HTTP or throw at the outer boundary only.
60s: Result makes failures visible in the signature. CSV bad rows return err, not throw. Erased at runtime — tsc enforces handling. C# mirrors with TryParse and small structs.
Follow-up: how is Promise<Result<T,E>> different from try/catch in async handlers?
commonPitfalls: Accessing .value without checking .ok — runtime undefined on failure branch.
Result-wrapping every npm throw instead of catching once at the edge.
Strong answer: 'Discriminated union, E as typed codes, map/flatMap chain, single HTTP conversion, metrics on err rate not exception rate.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS often uses null for failure and throw for exceptional — Result unifies both into an explicit union TypeScript can check.
C# TryParse and generic Result structs mirror { ok, value, error }. C# keeps a real struct at runtime; TS unions erase.
